topic.name: Solving Quadratic Equations Using a Difference of Squares

question.text: Use the difference of squares method to solve the equation $49j^2- 64=0.$
question.explanation:
Using the difference of squares formula, we factor the left-hand side of our quadratic equation: \begin{align*} 49j^2-64 &=0\\[5pt] (7j)^2-8^2 &= 0\\[5pt] (7j-8)(7j+8) &=0 \end{align*}

Applying the zero product rule, we have \[ 7j-8 =0 \qquad\text{or}\qquad 7j+8=0. \]

Then, we solve each equation separately: \begin{align*} 7j-8 &=0 &\qquad&\qquad& 7j+8&=0 \\[5pt] 7j &=8 &\qquad&\qquad& 7j&=-8 \\[5pt] j &=\dfrac{8}{7} &\qquad&\qquad& j&=-\dfrac{8}{7} \end{align*}

Therefore, the solutions are $j=-\dfrac{8}{7},\dfrac{8}{7}.$ We can write this even more concisely as $ j=\pm \dfrac{8}{7}.$

example.title: Solving Perfect Square Quadratic Equations With Leading Coefficients

question.text: Use the difference of squares method to solve the equation $4k^2-36 =0.$
question.explanation:
Before we start our normal process of factoring, notice that all of the terms have a common factor of $4.$ Therefore, we can simplify the expression by factoring out $4,$ as follows: \[ 4k^2 - 36 = 4(k^2 - 9) \]

Now, let's factor the expression inside parentheses using the difference of squares formula: \begin{align*} 4(k^2 - 9) & = 0\\[5pt] 4(k^2 - 3^2) & = 0\\[5pt] 4(k-3)(k+3) & = 0 \end{align*}

Applying the zero product rule, we have \[ k-3 =0 \qquad\text{or}\qquad k+3=0, \] which in turn gives \[ k=3 \qquad\text{or}\qquad k=-3. \]

Therefore, the solutions are $k=-3,3.$ We can write this even more concisely as $k =\pm3.$

question.text: Use the difference of squares method to solve the equation $4x^2=25.$
question.explanation:
First, we move all of the terms to the left-hand side and collect the like terms: \begin{align*} 4x^2 &= 25 \\[5pt] 4x^2 - 25 &= 0 \end{align*}

Now, using the difference of squares formula, we factor the left-hand side of our quadratic equation: \begin{align*} 4x^2 - 25 &= 0 \\[5pt] (2x)^2 - (5)^2 &= 0 \\[5pt] (2x-5)(2x+5) &= 0 \end{align*}

Applying the zero product rule, we have \[ 2x-5=0 \qquad\text{or}\qquad 2x+5=0. \]

Then, we solve each equation separately:

\begin{align*} 2x-5&=0 &\qquad&\qquad& 2x+5&=0 \\[5pt] 2x&=5 &\qquad&\qquad& 2x&=-5 \\[5pt] x&=\dfrac{5}{2} &\qquad&\qquad& x&=-\dfrac{5}{2} \end{align*}

Therefore, the solutions are $x=-\dfrac{5}{2},\dfrac{5}{2}.$ We can write this even more concisely as $x=\pm\dfrac{5}{2}.$
